newsitem.title: GERMANY: Outlook uncertain for more German pensions talks.
newsitem.headline: Outlook uncertain for more German pensions talks.

text.p: Germany's battered tradition of consensus politics took another blow on Tuesday as government and opposition emerged from talks on pensions reform with conflicting views on chances for a compromise.
Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, speaking after exploratory talks with the Social Democrats (SPD), said he expected formal negotiations on his pensions-cutting plans to go ahead.
"We will try to reach agreement," Bluem said after talks lasting two-and-a-half hours.
But SPD pensions expert Rudolf Dressler came out of the same meeting saying full-scale talks may not go ahead at all.
"The SPD executive must decide next Monday on whether to begin formal negotiations. I have no recommendation to make," Dressler said.
State pensions, created in the nineteenth century by united Germany's first chancellor Otto von Bismarck, have long been a policy issue dealt with on a non-partisan basis.
But the threat to the system posed by the "greying" of Germany's 80 million population -- coupled with the huge costs of unification in 1990 -- have broken that broad consensus.

Next year's general election has also cast a shadow over the effort to reach a compromise, even though both sides want to keep the pay-as-you-go system intact and reject calls to create a capital stock to contain pensions costs.
Bluem's plan seeks to balance the books by cutting typical pensions over the next generation to 64 percent of average net wages -- a level last seen in the 1970s -- from 70 percent now.
Transferring around 15 billion marks in non-welfare items from the pensions fund to the federal budget would make it possible to cut contributions from today's record 20.3 percent.
"The goal of the reform must be to relieve pensions insurance by saving and refinancing at the same time," Bluem said.

The SPD, in a policy document published at the weekend, rejected outright any cuts in pensions. In order to keep the system afloat it wants to get low-paid workers, who are now exempt, to pay pensions contributions.

The SPD also wants 30 billion marks -- including the cost of pensions paid to ethnic German immigrants from eastern Europe -- to be borne by the taxpayer. Both are mulling increases in indirect taxes to pay for their reforms.

That would dilute separate coalition plans to cut income and corporate taxes which the SPD has threatened to block in the Bundesrat upper house of parliament after cross-party talks collapsed in acrimony recently.
The SPD is not able to block pensions legislation.
Dressler said the exploratory talks had only served to reveal how far apart the two sides were.
"Regrettably, the only revelation of the talks was that the coalition said it was ready to discuss SPD proposals. This is a bare minimum," he said.
